newsitem.title: USA: U.S. airlines post mix earnings, hurt by tax.
newsitem.headline: U.S. airlines post mix earnings, hurt by tax.

text.p: U.S. airlines posted mixed second quarter earnings, as the federal excise tax and fare wars dampened domestic profits and offset strong international growth.
"On the international side, revenue and volume growth has been strong. But the continued effect of the ticket tax has hurt domestically," said Timothy Ross, an airline analyst with SBC Warburg.

The 10 percent passenger excise tax was not in place during last year's second quarter, which gave the airlines a windfall of funds that would normally go to the Federal Aviation Administration. Airlines had a tough time beating last year's inflated revenues, analysts said.

Although most airlines exceeded Wall Street expectations, four major carriers earned less money than they did a year ago. The mixed second quarter results contrasted the industry's 445 percent year-over-year earnings growth in the first quarter, according to a report by Natwest Securities.
Trans World Airlines Inc and ValuJet Inc, which have both struggled to return to profitability since last year's crashes, continued to lose money, posting greater-than-expected second quarter losses.
But TWA was "cautiously optimistic" it may return to profitability in the third quarter.
Delta Air Lines Inc also failed to meet analysts' expectations in the June quarter despite higher operating revenues and lower costs.

Last month, many analysts had trimmed their expectations on Delta's earnings after the nation's third largest carrier said that the ticket tax and an increase in lower-paying leisure travelers would pressure fourth quarter results.
But Delta still failed to meet Wall Street's lowered expectations, as operating income dropped nine percent from a year ago.

In addition to the ticket tax, Delta and US Airways Group Inc faced continued competition from low-cost carriers in the June quarter, analysts said. Low-cost carriers, such as Southwest Airlines Co, have also begun to encroach on the transcontinental market that the major carriers have historically had for themselves.

On Thursday, Southwest topped Wall Street expectations, with second quarter earnings of $0.62 a share, or $93.8 million, on revenues of $956.9 million. In the 1996 quarter, the company earned $0.56 per share, or $85.3 million, on revenues of $910.3 million.
Despite the ticket tax, Southwest said it benefitted from lower aircraft engine repair costs, lower jet fuel prices and internal cost reduction efforts.
Southwest expects its third quarter results to top the year ago performance, but said it would be "difficult" to match the better-than-expected performance seen in the second quarter.
"The second quarter is typically our strongest," the company said.
For others, the third quarter is shaping up to be a repeat of the second quarter.

Continental Airlines Inc, UAL Corp's United Airlines and AMR Corp's American each expect their third quarter performance to echo the second quarter, with international results outpacing domestic performance.

"I think on the domestic side, we're going to have a bit of a challenge, but the strength in the international operations will mitigate much of the potential weakness," said American Airlines chief financial officer Gerald Arpey.
